title: Keeping Time with the Skies

standard_text: Days, months and years from the motions of the Earth and Moon; lunar, solar and lunisolar calendars; leap years; the extra month in Indian calendars; the Indian national (Saka) calendar; the panchang and ancient Indian astronomy (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 11).
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 8 Science worksheets for NCERT Curiosity Chapter 11: days, months and years, lunar and solar calendars, leap years, lunisolar calendars and the extra month, and the Indian national calendar. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The Earth's spin gives the day; the Moon the month; the orbit the year.
key_sub: A leap year every 4 years keeps the calendar in step.
body_html:
How to think about it

A day comes from the Earth's rotation, a month from the Moon's cycle of phases (about 29.5 days) and a year from the Earth's revolution (about 365¼ days). The extra quarter days add up to a leap day every four years; in the Gregorian calendar a century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by 400.

Twelve lunar months make about 354 days, about 11 days less than a solar year, so festivals of a purely lunar calendar move earlier each year. Indian lunisolar calendars add an extra month (adhik maas) about every three years. India's national calendar is the Saka calendar, adopted in 1957, which begins on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

Example

Is 1900 a leap year?

century year not divisible by 400

Answer: no

Example

12 lunar months ≈ ?

12 × 29.5

Answer: 354 days

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every year divisible by 4 is a leap year, even 1900.
  • Mixing up the lunar month and the solar year.
  • Thinking festivals of lunar calendars fall on the same date each year.
